kin.note: THE NOTICE NAMES THE FATHER, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE OF WHAT IS CLAIMED. The Chicago Democrat of 3 December 1833, column 7: 'Mark Nobles, Esq. of this place, to Miss CHARLOTTE, only daughter of Mr. Charles Wesencraft, late of Buffalo'. Both cards were minted from that same reading of that same notice, so nothing is being identified by name here. 'Only daughter' is the paper's own word and no second daughter is implied. Ruled in data/residents/kin_rulings.json under 'hh_wesencraft_charles__daughter__charlotte' (T-1134).

merge_ruling.for_merge: THE STEM IS ALL BUT UNIQUE AND THE TOWN HAS ONE CHARLES OF EACH SPELLING. Charles Wesencraft is documented: the Democrat of 3 December 1833, column 7, prints the marriage of 'Mark Nobles, Esq. of this place, to Miss CHARLOTTE, only daughter of Mr. Charles Wesencraft, late of Buffalo', and his daughter Charlotte stands on her own card; Fergus 1843 prints 'Wesencraft, Charles, carpenter and wagon[maker], cor S. Clinton and W. Monroe' and Norris 1844 repeats the trade. 'Wessencraft, Charles' stands on the 1833 tax list. A carpenter and wagonmaker marrying a daughter into the Noble family in December 1833 is a man the town's tax roll of that year should hold.
merge_ruling.against_merge: NO TITLE SETS BOTH, AND THE DOUBLE-S IS NOT A ONE-OFF SLIP — A SECOND, LATER TITLE SETS IT TOO. Searched over every deposited text: 'Wessencraft' occurs twice in the whole corpus and the two are independent — 'Wessencraft, Charles' on the 1833 tax list (line 159) and 'Wessencraft, Mrs. Jane' on the Second Presbyterian Church roll of 1842-1892 (line 7270). Two documents sixty years apart, neither derived from the other, both doubling the S. Against them the Democrat, Fergus 1839, Fergus 1843 and Norris 1844 set the single S and never the double. The two bodies of evidence do not touch, and a spelling attested by two unrelated sources is exactly the kind a fold should not quietly absorb. D7, and the cards stay two. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT IS NOT A PAGE BUT A COUNT, in C12's shape moved from the forename to the surname — the closed roll leaves the documented man exactly one entry he can be, and the exhaustion is worked over the whole roll and printed rather than asserted. C12 as written reaches a FORENAME only, so firing it on a surname is itself a rule to write. T-1135 owns that question for Pruyne/Pryne and the rule it writes is the one this pair waits on.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. WHAT THIS PASS RULED ONTO THIS HOUSEHOLD, named so the ruling can be found again: each volume below is followed by the printed entries it set against this person and the status the crosswalk ruled them at — a single entry carries what its own `could_carry` declares, and an ambiguous or contested match carries nothing and is shown so that the silence is legible. wesencraft_charles, Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 — f1839_e1580 (a single entry); wesencraft_charles, Fergus's Chicago directory of 1843 — f1843_e2582 (a single entry); wesencraft_charles, Norris's Chicago directory of 1844 — n1844_e1875 (a single entry).

occupation_later.note: Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints this trade against this person, in the entry quoted on the card: 'Wesencraft, Chas. , carpenter and wagonmaker, Clinton c. Monroe'. It is evidence about 1839, written here as 1839's and read back onto no 1835 claim. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. The value is the volume's own line, split by its crosswalk on the entry's punctuation. These volumes set the trade first and its qualifiers after it on the same line, so the split may carry an employer, a market or a corner along with the trade. The printed entry is quoted beside the value for exactly that reason: the split is checkable against it, and neither is read into an 1835 claim.
